description: Append-only Analyst timeline. Reset 2026-07-27 when the baseline, the reabsorption axis and the falsifier format all changed; earlier entries were scored against a rolling baseline and are not comparable. Archived under archive/.

entries.notificationLine: New results are in: displacement verdict as AI-exposed industries shed jobs while others hire

falsifier.unit: percentage points of the 25-54 population, 12-month change

entries.falsifierPlain: The prime-age employment-rate chart moves first — if its 12-month change climbs back to -0.2 or better while the exposed-minus-control jobs gap narrows to -1.75 or above by late October, then what I am calling displacement was reallocation plus the tail of the 2021-22 hiring correction.
entries.analysis:
The reading is displacement, early and only moderately supported. It rests on deterioration that is actually visible rather than on the absence of bad news: the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is falling, unemployment spells are getting longer, and the industries most exposed to AI are the ones shedding jobs.

The strongest evidence is where the job losses sit. Employment in information, professional and business services, and finance — where AI can do the most of the work — is down 1.3% over the past year. Employment in construction, leisure and hospitality, and education and health, where AI touches very little of the day, is up 1.3%. Both sides are moving, in opposite directions. That matters because it rules out a general slowdown: if the whole economy were cooling, construction and health care would be cooling too, and instead their pay is growing 3.5% a year and their job postings sit about 4% above where they were in February 2020. Unemployment overall is 4.2%, payrolls added 57,000 in the latest month, and bond markets are not pricing a downturn. Whatever is pulling exposed employment down is specific to those industries.

The problem is that the same split is exactly what successful reallocation looks like. If a hundred jobs move from information to health care, exposed employment falls, other employment rises, and nobody is displaced. So the question is whether people leaving are landing. Two signals say landing has got harder. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds in work is 80.2%, down half a point over the year — and the entire decline arrived in the last quarter, after nine roughly flat months. The share of unemployed people out of work more than six months is 27.3%, up 4 points over the year.

Both of those come with honest caveats that keep this call moderate rather than strong. That 80.2% is still about a quarter of a point above its 2019 level, near the top of its historical range, and a half-point annual fall is close to an ordinary year in the 2010s given how much this series normally moves. The long-term unemployment share can also rise for a harmless reason: short spells ending faster while long spells hold steady.

The strongest case against the displacement reading is three findings, none of them older than the evidence supporting it.

Job postings. Postings for knowledge work sit about 24% below their February 2020 level, while postings for hands-on work sit about 4% above theirs. That is a large hole — but it is filling in, narrowing by 3 points over six months and well off its worst point in late 2023. Postings lead hiring, so a recovering postings series argues the worst is behind. This is the most recent evidence available, which means the strongest counterweight here is newer than the case for displacement, not older.

Pay. Wages in the AI-heavy industries are growing 4.6% a year against 3.5% where AI has barely arrived. Faster pay growth where AI is heaviest is backwards from a story about those workers being replaced. I am not treating it as evidence of augmentation, for one reason: employment in those industries is shrinking about 1.3%, and when a workforce shrinks the average wage rises mechanically as lower-paid people leave, with nobody getting a raise. But my reading runs against the direction of this evidence, and a reader who thinks that composition effect is small should treat the pay gap as real evidence that AI is making these workers more valuable.

Hiring flows. Hiring runs at 3.3% of employment a month, voluntary quitting at 1.9%, and that margin has improved slightly over the year. Both legs are low, though: few people hired, few choosing to leave. The net looks healthy partly because quitting is subdued, not because hiring is strong.

There is a full non-AI explanation with real evidence behind it. Information, professional services and finance over-hired in 2021 and 2022 and have been unwinding ever since. That explains the worst of the sectoral gap in late 2023, the long stretch of weak knowledge-work postings, and the low-churn market. What it explains less well is why exposed employment is still outright falling four to five years in. A hiring correction is a one-time adjustment to a level — employment should flatten out lower, not keep declining after postings, the correction's own leading indicator, have already turned up. That unexplained remainder is why this is not filed as an unresolvable confound. The hiring correction carries more than half of what we can see. I do not think it carries all of it.

Two figures often cited here cover every worker in the country, not the exposed industries, and cannot be used as evidence about them. Output per hour is growing 2.8% a year, the fastest since the internet boom. Labour's share of all income generated in the economy is 51.0%, the lowest in records going back to 1947, down a full point over four quarters against a long-run drift of about a tenth of a point a year. Production is getting more efficient, the gains are not reaching wages, and it is happening without a recession — but rising output per hour is equally the signature of workers being made more valuable, so on its own it settles nothing.

Watch the prime-age employment rate. If the drop that arrived in the last quarter reverses, the foundation of this displacement reading goes with it.
entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, at an early stage, and it is only moderately supported. It rests on deterioration that is actually visible in the data rather than on the absence of bad news: the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is falling, unemployment spells are getting longer, and both of those are happening while the industries most exposed to AI are the ones losing jobs. That is a positive claim about damage, not a claim that nothing has gone wrong yet. A careful reader looking at the same evidence could call this reallocation instead — workers moving from one kind of job to another with nobody ending up idle — and would not be being unreasonable. The rest of this explains why displacement is the better fit and where the case is thin.

Start with the split that gives the reading its shape. Employment in information, professional and business services, and finance — the three industries where AI can do the most of the work — is down 1.3% over the past year, as of June 2026. Employment in construction, leisure and hospitality, and education and health, where AI touches very little of the day, is up 1.3% over the same year. Both sides are moving, in opposite directions, which is why the gap between them is as wide as it has been at any point outside late 2023. Set against how these two groups normally behave relative to each other in the decade before 2020, this is a genuinely unusual configuration, and it has now been unusual for two months running. It is worth saying that it is not getting worse: the gap was fractionally wider a month ago. The divergence is holding, not accelerating.

The most important thing this split does is rule out a general slowdown. If the whole economy were cooling, construction, hospitality and health care would be cooling too. They are not. Their job growth is positive, their pay is growing 3.5% a year, and job postings in hands-on work sit about 4% above where they were in February 2020. Unemployment overall is 4.2% and payrolls added 57,000 in the latest month. Bond markets are not pricing a downturn either — the ten-year Treasury yields more than the two-year, which is the normal, non-recessionary arrangement. So whatever is pulling down employment in the exposed industries is specific to those industries, not the weather over the whole economy.

That is the strength of the case. Here is the weakness, and it is real. The same split is exactly what a successful reallocation looks like. If a hundred jobs move out of information and into health care, exposed employment falls, control employment rises, the gap widens from both ends, and not one worker is displaced. Control industries adding jobs at 1.3% is precisely the destination such a flow would need. The industry grouping is also crude: a janitor employed by a software company counts as exposed, a data analyst at a factory does not.

So the question becomes whether the people leaving the exposed industries are landing somewhere. That is where the deterioration shows up, and where it is smaller than the word "displacement" suggests. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds in work is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months. Two things about that number pull in opposite directions. Against it: 80.2% is still about a quarter of a point above where it stood in 2019, near the top of its historical range, and a half-point annual decline is close to an ordinary year in the 2010s by the normal year-to-year variation in this series. A reader who recomputes from the historical spread will get a milder answer than the dashboard's own scoring gives, and that is part of why I am calling this moderate rather than strong. For it: the entire half-point decline arrived in the most recent quarter. Prime-age employment was roughly flat for nine months and then gave up half a point in three. A level measured against 2019 is slow to register a fresh turn when it starts from a high place, and that is the situation here.

The second absorption signal is the share of the unemployed who have been out of work more than six months: 27.3%, up 4 points over the past year. The direction is clearly bad — people who lose jobs are waiting longer to find new ones. The magnitude is not yet abnormal; swings of four points in a year are common in this series. This number also has an honest alternative explanation. A share can rise because short spells are ending faster while long spells hold steady, with nobody's prospects actually worsening. And a market with little hiring and little quitting lengthens spells for everyone regardless of cause.

That brings me to the strongest single thing arguing against the displacement reading, which is a cluster of three findings, all of them either fresher than or as fresh as the evidence supporting it.

First, job postings. Postings for knowledge work sit about 24% below their February 2020 level; postings for hands-on work sit about 4% above theirs. That is a large hole. But the hole is filling in, not deepening: the gap has narrowed by 3 points over the last six months and is well off its worst point in late 2023. Postings lead hiring by months, so a recovering postings series is a forward-looking argument that the worst is behind. This is the most recent panel on the board, from July 2026, which means the strongest counterweight to my reading is newer than the evidence supporting it. I cannot dismiss it on grounds of staleness. If AI were progressively eating knowledge work, postings in knowledge work should be making new lows, not clawing back.

Second, pay. Wages in the exposed industries are growing 4.6% a year against 3.5% in the control industries. Faster pay growth where AI is heaviest is backwards from a story about those workers being replaced, and on its face it is the augmentation evidence. I am not treating it as such, for one specific reason: employment in those industries is shrinking by about 1.3%, and when a workforce shrinks, the average wage rises mechanically as lower-paid people leave, with nobody getting a raise. The control side compounds it, because leisure and hospitality is low-paid and growing, which drags the control average down. So the pay gap cannot tell augmentation from displacement here. But I want to be plain: my reading runs against the direction of this panel, and I am setting it aside on a measurement rule, not because it points my way. A reader who thinks the composition effect is small should treat it as real evidence of augmentation, and my reading would be hard to sustain against it.

Third, the flow of people through jobs. Hiring runs at 3.3% of employment a month and voluntary quitting at 1.9%, so hiring exceeds quitting by 1.4 points, and that margin has improved slightly over the year. On its face that is fine. But both legs are low. This is a market where few people are being hired and few are choosing to leave. The net looks healthy partly because quitting is subdued, not because hiring is strong. A low-hiring market and a lengthening queue of long-term unemployed are the same fact seen twice: anyone who does leave waits longer to land.

Now the competing explanation that has a real series behind it. Information, professional services and finance hired heavily in 2021 and 2022 and have been unwinding that ever since. This account explains a great deal. It explains the deepest point of the exposed-versus-control gap, which was in November 2023. It explains why knowledge-work postings have been below their pre-pandemic level continuously since. It explains the low-churn market, because a sector that over-hired stops hiring and its workers stop quitting. What it explains less well is why exposed employment is still outright falling, at 1.3% a year, four to five years in. A hiring correction is a one-time adjustment to a level; you would expect employment to flatten out lower, not to keep declining after the correction's own leading indicator — postings — has already turned up. That is the residual, and it is the reason I did not call this confounded. Mixed evidence is not the same as a competing cause that explains the data better. I concede the hiring correction carries more than half of what we can see. I do not think it carries all of it.

Two more panels, and both need a warning attached. Output per hour worked is growing 2.8% a year as of March 2026, up from 2.5%, the first quarter inside the range last seen during the internet boom. And labour's share of all income generated in the economy is 51.0%, the lowest in records going back to 1947, having fallen a full point over four quarters against a long-run drift of roughly a tenth of a point a year. Both of these are economy-wide figures covering every worker in the country. Neither can be used as evidence about what is happening in the AI-exposed industries specifically, and I have not paired them with the exposed-industry job figures as though they described the same group of workers. What they establish is context: production is getting more efficient, the gains are not reaching wages, and this is happening without a recession. Faster productivity with shrinking exposed employment is the arithmetic signature of the same work being done with fewer hours — but it is equally the arithmetic signature of workers being made more valuable. It does not discriminate on its own, and it is a quarter older than the labour figures.

I considered and set aside several other explanations. A war-driven shock to hiring, following the Iran conflict, is a genuine hypothesis, but the sectoral pattern is wrong: an energy-and-confidence shock should hit construction and hospitality at least as hard as finance, and those industries are growing. Inflation and interest rates are unremarkable — expected inflation over ten years is 2.3% — so there is no demand shock big enough to knock three specific industries into decline while three others expand. And there is nothing in economy-wide payrolls or the 4.2% unemployment rate that discriminates between the two readings; both a slow-but-positive aggregate with a shrinking exposed sector, and early displacement partly masked by growth elsewhere, look like that.

On why not augmentation: calling it augmentation requires positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable. The only candidate is the pay gap, which the shrinking-workforce problem disqualifies. Productivity is economy-wide and cannot speak to exposed industries. The one survey that measures whether firms use AI to automate or to assist — it splits roughly 43% automation to 57% assistance, and has barely moved across its three releases — is ten months old and cannot describe how AI is being used in mid-2026. The weaker claim, that displacement simply has not started, is more defensible than augmentation, and it fails only narrowly: it needs an absence of deterioration, and prime-age employment and long-term unemployment are both deteriorating on the freshest readings available.

For completeness: AI adoption reached 21.7% of firms in July 2026, up from 17.3% in November 2025, with firms of 250 or more employees at 38.8% against 20.8% for the very smallest. Adoption is wide enough for a displacement reading to be possible; it does not cause anything and I have used it only as a gate. Recent graduates face an unemployment rate 2.6 points above the general rate, above its own ten-year average, but graduates have fared worse than the general workforce for 150 straight months, so this carries almost no weight.

What would change my mind, and by when. I want a test the hiring-correction explanation cannot pass on its own, which means a joint condition on recovery, because displacement produces neither leg while a finished correction produces both. If by late October 2026 the annual change in prime-age employment has recovered to roughly a fifth of a point of decline or better — meaning the single-quarter drop reversed and the aggregate is absorbing people again — and at the same time the gap between exposed and control job growth has narrowed to around 1.75 points from today's 2.5, back within normal range for these two groups, then what I am calling displacement was reallocation plus the tail of the 2021-22 hiring correction. Sustained displacement does not produce a recovering employment rate and a closing sectoral gap at the same time. A correction that has finished produces exactly that.

I rejected two simpler tests. A threshold on the postings gap is useless, because that gap reached its worst level in late 2023, during the hiring correction, so any line drawn in that region would fire on a second correction just as readily as on displacement. And a test on prime-age employment alone is useless, because that number falls in every ordinary cooling — its worst pre-2020 reading came in the middle of an expansion.

The single chart to watch is the prime-age employment rate. If the drop that arrived in the last quarter reverses, the case I have made loses its foundation.

compliance.lengthBand: extended (a month with something to explain)

entries.confidenceBasis: Corroborating: exposed_vs_control_jobs (as_of 2026-06, differential -2.54, past its -2.48 trigger and 2.08 SD past the clean pre-2020 baseline, with control industries at +1.27% so the contemporaneous macro test does not explain it) and reabsorption (as_of 2026-06, headline prime-age employment share 12-month change -0.5 against a pre-2020 norm of +0.42/SD 0.52, i.e. well past the panel's 1-SD deterioration rule, with the decomposition showing prime-age employment itself down 1.38% and the long-term-unemployed share up 4.0 points to 27.3%); adoption gate passed (21.7% of firms, 38.8% at 250+ employees). Failing to corroborate or cutting against: job_postings_spread (as_of 2026-07, the freshest and the leading panel, spread narrowing +3.9 over six months), reabsorption's own JOLTS readouts (layoffs 1.1 and flat, hires-minus-quits +0.1 — a frozen market, not a shedding one), individual_wage_growth (switcher premium 0.8, above its pre-2020 mean, so movers are still landing well), labor_productivity (2.8%, in the internet-boom band). Two of the three doubts are unmet and I am publishing anyway: the headline's entire 12-month deterioration sits inside the last three months (3-month change also -0.5), and the leading indicator (postings) is pointing the other way.
entries.notificationLine: Displacement holds on a flat month; new job-switcher pay data is the strongest counter.

falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in the share of 25-54-year-olds with a job)

entries.falsifierPlain: If the prime-age employment-rate chart in the reabsorption panel climbs back so its 12-month change is no worse than -0.1 while the long-term-unemployed share falls back to 26% or below, people are landing again and this displacement reading was wrong.
entries.analysis:
The reading is displacement, and it rests on something happening rather than on the absence of good news: jobs in AI-exposed industries are actually shrinking, by 1.27% over the past year, while jobs in the control industries AI has barely touched grew 1.27%, and the people coming out are not landing again.

Nothing moved this month. The jobs gap between exposed and control industries shifted by four hundredths of a point, pay growth on each side by a hundredth, the share of firms using AI not at all. The household and payroll figures still run through June, so every labour reading is the one from last month. The reading rests on levels that were already there, not on fresh deterioration, and that is worth saying plainly rather than dressing up a flat month.

The one new thing is a measure that follows the same individuals over time, and it argues against displacement — see below.

What makes this displacement rather than workers reshuffling between industries is the absorption side. The share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job has fallen half a percentage point over twelve months, in a series that normally rises about four-tenths of a point a year, and prime-age employment itself is down about 1.4 million people, so this is not an artefact of a growing population. The share of unemployed people out of work six months or longer has climbed four points to 27.3%. If only the exposed industries were weak, that would be reallocation. People staying unemployed longer is what turns it into displacement.

Three things cut the other way and one of them is new.

Postings for knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on work sit about 4% above theirs — but that gap has been closing, by 3.9 points over six months and nine-tenths in the last month. Closing is what recovery looks like. This is the freshest data on the board, a month ahead of everything supporting the displacement reading, and it points the other way. One caveat readers deserve: the published figures show the change in the gap but not in each side separately, so it is impossible to tell whether knowledge-work postings are recovering or hands-on postings are falling back. If it is the second, the narrowing is not good news at all.

The new individual-level pay data shows people who change jobs still getting about eight-tenths of a point more wage growth than people who stay, above the pre-2020 norm of six-tenths and recovering. That is people moving because they see something better, not because they were pushed. It covers the whole workforce, including exposed workers, so it cannot be waved away as measuring the wrong people. It is a median, though, so a collapse concentrated in a minority is exactly what it would miss.

And layoffs are entirely normal, at 1.1% of employment, while hiring is weak. That combination is not an economy shedding workers, it is one that has stopped taking people in. A frozen market has a perfectly good explanation in interest rates, and its burden falls mainly on people entering work, who are mostly under 25 and mostly outside the prime-age figures above.

There is also a real residual to be honest about. Information and professional services overhired badly in 2021 and 2022 and have been unwinding since, and that explains why these gaps opened. It does not explain why they are still here. An unwind decays; four years on, exposed employment is not just below trend but contracting outright, while the controls — which also overhired, in leisure and hospitality — are growing. That leftover is what this reading is built on, and it is a thinner thing than the headline gap suggests.

Two figures that get quoted as evidence do not belong here. Productivity growth at 2.8% a year and the worker share of national income at a record-low 51.0% both cover the whole economy, not AI-exposed work, and output per hour rises mechanically whenever hours are cut faster than output falls. Neither tells augmentation and displacement apart.

What to watch: the prime-age employment rate in the reabsorption panel. If it turns back up, people are landing again and this reading is wrong.
entries.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is a positive reading rather than a reading resting on the absence of something. Two things have to be true at once for me to say displacement rather than reshuffling, and both are on the board. First, something is happening specifically to AI-exposed work: employment in AI-exposed industries is shrinking by 1.27% over the past year while employment in the control industries AI has barely touched is growing by 1.27%. Second, the wider labour market is not catching the people coming out: the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job has fallen half a percentage point over twelve months, in a series that normally rises about four-tenths of a point a year, and the share of unemployed people who have been out of work six months or longer has climbed four points to 27.3%. If only the first were true, this would be reallocation — one set of industries shrinking, another growing, workers moving between them. It is the second that makes it displacement.

Nothing meaningful moved this month. The exposed-versus-control jobs gap shifted by four hundredths of a point, exposed and control pay growth each moved by a hundredth, the share of firms using AI was unchanged at 21.7%, and the postings gap closed by nine-tenths of a point. Every underlying labour reading is the same one as last month, because the household and payroll data still run through June. So the reading rests on levels that were already there, not on fresh deterioration, and I would rather say that plainly than dress a quiet month up as a development. The one genuinely new thing on the board is a measure of pay growth that follows the same individuals over time, and it argues against displacement. More on that below.

Taking the panels one at a time.

Jobs in exposed versus control industries. Naming both sides rather than the gap: the exposed side is in outright contraction, down 1.27% year over year, and the control side is growing at 1.27%. That combination is what rules out a general downturn. If this were the ordinary business cycle, construction, leisure and hospitality, and education and health would be weak too, and they are not — they are the ones adding jobs. Interest rates are not signalling recession either, though I am not leaning on that in either direction; a signal that says "no recession" cannot explain away weakness that is visibly there. What the control-industry strength buys me is specificity: whatever is hitting information and professional services is not hitting the whole economy. What it does not buy me is displacement over reallocation. That comes from the absorption evidence.

The strongest argument against the exposed-jobs finding is the hiring correction. Information and professional and business services hired far too aggressively in 2021 and 2022 and have been letting that unwind ever since. The postings data carries its own note saying the exposed-versus-control gap in job advertisements opened in 2022 and attributes a substantial part of it to the interest-rate cycle rather than to anything models did. That explains the opening of both gaps, and probably a fair part of why exposed employment is still below where its old trend would have put it in 2026. What it does not explain is why the gap is still here. An unwind decays. Four years on, the exposed side is not merely below trend, it is contracting year over year, while the controls — which also overhired, in leisure and hospitality — are growing. That leftover is what I am reading. It is a smaller thing than the raw two-and-a-half-point gap suggests, and I want that said rather than buried.

A limitation of the exposed-versus-control split worth stating: exposure is assigned by industry, not by job. A janitor in a software firm counts as exposed; a data analyst in a factory does not. The job-postings panel, which is cut by occupation, is the better measure of who is actually exposed — and it points the other way.

Job postings. This is the freshest panel on the board, running through July, a month ahead of everything supporting the displacement reading. Postings for knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level, while postings for hands-on work sit about 4% above theirs. That is a wide gap, and on level alone it supports the reading. But the level is old news and the movement is what matters: the gap has closed by 3.9 points over six months and by nine-tenths in the last month. Closing is what recovery, or genuine augmentation, would look like. There is a hole in this I cannot fill from what I have: I am given the change in the gap but not the change in each side separately, so I cannot tell whether knowledge-work postings are recovering or hands-on postings are falling back. If it is the latter, the narrowing is not good news at all. Either way, the panel most likely to turn first is turning against the displacement reading, and it is newer than the evidence for it. That is the single biggest reason I am not stating this with high confidence.

Absorption. The level of prime-age employment is not alarming — 80.2% of 25-to-54-year-olds have a job, which is fractionally above where it stood in 2019. The direction is what is bad. The twelve-month change is minus half a point, against a norm of gently rising. Almost the whole of that move happened in the most recent quarter, which means this is one quarter of evidence rather than a year of it, and one quarter can be noise.

I checked whether the employment rate is falling because employment is falling or because the population it is divided by is rising. Employment itself is down 1.38%, about 1.4 million prime-age people, so the ratio is not deteriorating merely on arithmetic. I am deliberately not quoting the population side: the January Census population controls put a plus-1.9-million level shift into this series in 2025 and a minus-1.5-million shift in 2026, which makes the population leg unusable for measuring anything. Only the direction of the employment leg survives, and that was the piece I needed.

The long-term unemployed share is the other absorption reading I lean on, at 27.3% and up four points on the year. It matters because it is a share of the unemployed rather than a share of the population, which makes it largely immune to the population-control problem that damages the headline employment rate. People who lose exposed-industry jobs are staying unemployed longer.

Against that, the flow numbers say something different and I have to take it. Layoffs are running at 1.1% of employment and are flat, exactly where they normally sit. Hiring is weak at 3.3% and quits at 1.9%, and the gap between them has actually improved slightly over the year. Weak hiring plus normal layoffs is not an economy shedding workers, it is an economy that has stopped taking people in. That is a frozen market, and a frozen market has a perfectly good non-AI explanation in interest rates and business uncertainty. It also puts most of the burden on people trying to enter work, who are mostly under 25 and therefore mostly outside the 25-to-54 group the headline employment rate covers. This is the strongest competing story and it is doing part of the work here. It fails the same specificity test the cyclical story fails — a rate-driven freeze should be general, and the control industries are hiring — which is why I record it as the main thing weakening confidence rather than as grounds to call this month confounded. Mixed evidence is not the same as an identified alternative cause.

Pay in exposed versus control industries. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing faster than in control industries, 4.63% against 3.53%. On its face that is backwards for displacement. But this panel only means something when employment is holding up, and exposed employment is falling, so it cannot separate augmentation from displacement and I am not citing it as support for either. There is a specific reason to distrust it here: if entry-level hiring in exposed industries has stopped, the workforce that remains skews more senior and the average wage rises without anyone getting a raise. The economy-wide individual-level trackers sit at 3.6% for people who stay in their jobs and 4.4% for people who move — both well below 4.63% — which hints that the exposed-industry figure is partly composition. I cannot prove it, because those trackers cover the whole economy and cannot be cut to exposed industries. So the composition question stays open and the panel stays weak, in both directions.

The new panel: individual wage growth. This follows the same people over time, which is what makes it useful as a check on the composition problem above. People who change jobs are still earning about eight-tenths of a point more growth than people who stay, a premium above its pre-2020 average of about six-tenths, and it has been recovering over recent readings. That is the shape of people moving because they see something better, not because they were pushed. It is the cleanest single argument against the displacement reading, and unlike the productivity and labour-share numbers it cannot be dismissed as covering the wrong workers — it covers everyone, exposed workers included. Two things temper it without disposing of it. It is a median, so a collapse concentrated in a minority is precisely the shape it would miss. And the household survey behind it has been degrading, with October 2025 missing outright.

Productivity. Output per hour is growing at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, which sits at the low edge of the late-1990s internet-boom range for one quarter. Real aggregate gains showing up is what augmentation working looks like, and I take it seriously. Two things stop it from overturning the reading. It is economy-wide, so none of it can be attributed to AI-exposed work specifically. And output per hour is a ratio: it rises mechanically when hours are cut faster than output falls, so a firm producing the same with fewer people generates exactly this number. Rising productivity sitting on top of falling prime-age employment does not tell augmentation and displacement apart. This figure is also four months old, from the first quarter, against labour data running to June and July — a real gap, and worth flagging because this panel is the load-bearing piece of the augmentation counter-case.

Labour share of income. The share of national income going to workers rather than to capital has fallen to 51.0%, a new low for the full history, with four consecutive quarterly declines and a one-point fall over four quarters — a pace in the fastest tenth on record and many times the slow drift of the past forty years. Directionally this fits the displacement reading. I give it no weight in the verdict: it is economy-wide, it has no threshold, and on the historical record a measure like this fires in recessions, not on technology.

AI adoption. 21.7% of firms report using AI in some business function, up from 17.3% in November 2025, with large employers at 38.8% — so the share of workers in an AI-using firm is well above the share of firms. This establishes that AI use is now widespread enough that a labour effect is possible. It causes nothing and I am not treating its rise as evidence that anything has happened to workers.

Capability benchmarks. Read and counted in nothing. The leading model can now sustain tasks of a few hours' length at the measured reliability threshold, and on one professional-task benchmark models reached about 71% wins-plus-ties in December 2025 — though wins alone were just under half, and that is a lab reporting on its own benchmark with nothing published since. None of this is an event in anyone's employment.

Two alternatives I considered and rejected as the named cause. First, shrinking labour supply from immigration enforcement. If the prime-age population is genuinely falling, employment can fall with nobody being displaced. I reject it because the population series has been disqualified by its own documentation, as above, and because immigration-sensitive employment concentrates in construction and leisure and hospitality — the control industries, which are growing. A supply shock that spares the control side and hits information and professional services is the wrong shape. Second, the frozen hiring market, discussed above.

Two cross-panel oddities worth recording. The household survey says prime-age employment is down 1.38% over the year while the establishment survey says payrolls grew by 57,000 in the latest month and control industries grew 1.27% over the year. These are different surveys covering different things and it is wrong to net them against each other, but a disagreement that large is a reason to hold the household-based absorption reading loosely, particularly given the documented decline in household survey response rates. Separately, the headline employment rate's level says the market is fine and its change says it is deteriorating; that is expected, and the right way to read it is level for where we are, change for which way we are going. Overall the news picture is soft but positive: 57,000 jobs added, unemployment at 4.2%. A labour market destroying work wholesale does not usually add payrolls. That sits comfortably with the frozen-market story and uncomfortably with mine.

What would show the displacement reading is wrong. Absorption returning. Specifically: the prime-age employment rate climbing back so its twelve-month change is no worse than a tenth of a point down, while the long-term unemployed share falls back to 26% or below, by late October. The first says people are landing again; the second guards against a bounce that leaves the people already stranded still stranded. Both are reachable — the employment rate moved half a point in a single quarter, and the long-term share moved nearly two points in three months — and both publish monthly, so three more readings land before the deadline. I deliberately did not make the second test "the exposed-versus-control jobs gap closes." At its recent pace of movement it could not get to a meaningful level by October, and a test that cannot fire is worthless. It is also the wrong test: if people start landing while the industry gap stays open, that is reallocation with a functioning labour market, and reallocation is exactly the finding that would make a displacement reading wrong.
